questions.stem: An engineer resumes yesterday's session with `--resume auth-refactor`. Since then, they have edited `session.ts` and `tokens.ts` by hand. What is the most effective first message in the resumed session?

options.text: Tell Claude exactly which files changed (and ideally how), and ask it to re-read them before continuing.
options.why: A resumed session's earlier tool results are stale, so point it at the changes explicitly.

options.text: "Continue where we left off."
options.why: Claude would rely on the stale file contents in its history.

options.text: Paste the whole repository diff for the last month.
options.why: This creates excessive bloat. Be targeted.

options.text: Run `/compact` first.
options.why: Compaction doesn't refresh stale file contents.

questions.explanation: When resuming, inform the session about external file changes so it re-reads them rather than trusting stale context.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to "improve performance of the web app" with no further detail. What is the best way to approach this open-ended task?

options.text: First map the system (profile hot paths, bundle sizes, slow endpoints), prioritise the highest-impact areas, then tackle them in focused steps, adapting as findings come in.
options.why: Open-ended tasks call for adaptive decomposition: map, prioritise, adapt.

options.text: Start optimising the first file alphabetically.
options.why: Effort goes nowhere near the actual bottlenecks.

options.text: Rewrite the app in a faster framework.
options.why: This is a disproportionate, unvalidated change.

options.text: Refuse until the engineer writes a full specification.
options.why: Claude can investigate first, and use the interview pattern if needed.

questions.explanation: Decompose open-ended work adaptively: understand the structure, prioritise, then iterate.

questions.stem: The root CLAUDE.md should include the team's API style guide, which already exists as `docs/api-style.md`. What is the cleanest approach that avoids duplicating content?

options.text: Reference it from CLAUDE.md with an import line such as `@docs/api-style.md`.
options.why: `@import` reuses existing documents without duplicating them.

options.text: Copy the content into CLAUDE.md and keep both in sync by hand.
options.why: The two copies will drift.

options.text: Add the doc to `.mcp.json`.
options.why: That is MCP configuration, not memory.

options.text: Tell engineers to paste the doc at the start of each session.
options.why: This is manual and error-prone.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md supports `@path` imports for modular, non-duplicated memory.

questions.stem: Terraform conventions (naming, required tags, module layout) should apply only when Claude edits files under `infra/terraform/`. That directory has nested modules several levels deep. Which TWO options correctly scope these conventions? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A `.claude/rules/terraform.md` file with frontmatter `paths: ["infra/terraform/**/*"]`.
options.why: A path-scoped rule loads only for matching files.

options.text: A CLAUDE.md placed in `infra/terraform/`.
options.why: Directory-level memory applies when working within that tree, and these conventions follow the directory.

options.text: A section in the root CLAUDE.md headed "Terraform (only for infra files)".
options.why: It is always loaded, and scoping relies on the model's inference.

options.text: A personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/terraform`.
options.why: It isn't shared and needs to be invoked.

options.text: An entry in `.mcp.json`.
options.why: Unrelated to conventions.

questions.explanation: Both path-glob rules and directory CLAUDE.md work for conventions bounded by a directory. Glob rules are the choice when files are scattered.

questions.stem: The shared `/new-endpoint` command needs the endpoint name as input, and engineers keep forgetting the expected format. What helps most?

options.text: Use the command or skill's argument support (for example `$ARGUMENTS` in the body) and declare an `argument-hint` such as `<resource-name> [--auth]` so the expected input is shown.
options.why: Argument hints document the expected arguments inline.

options.text: Document the format in the README.
options.why: Engineers won't see it at the moment they invoke the command.

options.text: Split it into one command per resource.
options.why: This produces an explosion of commands.

options.text: Have the command guess the name from the branch name.
options.why: This is fragile.

questions.explanation: Commands and skills accept arguments, and `argument-hint` tells users what to pass.

questions.stem: Claude Code must trace how a `userId` flows through 25 wrapper modules before a change is made. What is the most context-efficient exploration strategy?

options.text: Build understanding incrementally: Grep for entry points, follow the usages through the wrappers step by step, and record the traced call chain in a notes file as you go.
options.why: Incremental, targeted exploration with persisted notes avoids context overload.

options.text: Read all 25 modules in full up front.
options.why: This floods the context.

options.text: Guess the flow from the module names.
options.why: This is unreliable.

options.text: Ask the engineer to draw the call graph.
options.why: The tool can do the tracing itself.

questions.explanation: Explore incrementally, trace usage across wrappers, and persist findings.

questions.stem: The assistant uses a coordinator with a "code-search" subagent and an "issue-tracker" subagent. For the question "why was the retry limit changed last quarter?", the coordinator only queries code-search and answers without the ticket history. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The coordinator's prompt or the subagent descriptions don't make clear when the issue-tracker subagent is relevant (for example "why/when was X changed" → ticket and PR history), so subagent selection failed.
options.why: Dynamic subagent selection depends on clear descriptions and criteria.

options.text: Subagents can't be used together in one task.
options.why: False. A coordinator can use several.

options.text: The issue tracker MCP server is too slow.
options.why: It was never called, so its speed isn't the cause.

options.text: The code-search subagent should have answered from commit messages alone.
options.why: This ignores the routing problem.

questions.explanation: Coordinators choose subagents dynamically from their descriptions and the coordinator's criteria. Unclear descriptions cause routing gaps.

questions.stem: Different MCP servers return timestamps and status values in inconsistent formats (`"DONE"`, `"closed"`, `3`). The agent makes mistakes when comparing them. What is the best place to fix this?

options.text: A PostToolUse hook that normalises the statuses to a canonical enum and the timestamps to ISO 8601 before the results reach the model.
options.why: Deterministic normalisation at the tool boundary removes the ambiguity.

options.text: A prompt section explaining every server's format.
options.why: This is probabilistic and has to be maintained for every server.

options.text: A request to each MCP vendor to change their formats.
options.why: This is slow and outside your control.

options.text: A second model that rewrites the agent's answers.
options.why: It costs more and fixes the problem late.

questions.explanation: Use PostToolUse hooks for data normalisation across heterogeneous tools.

questions.stem: Automated code changes must pass the test suite before the assistant opens a PR. Sometimes the assistant opens PRs without running tests. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Make the PR-creation tool (or a hook on it) refuse unless a test run for the current commit has passed, as recorded by the test tool.
options.why: A programmatic prerequisite gate guarantees the order of steps.

options.text: Add "always run tests before opening a PR" to the system prompt.
options.why: This is probabilistic.

options.text: Ask the assistant to state that tests passed in the PR description.
options.why: That is self-reported, not verified.

options.text: Let reviewers catch PRs without tests.
options.why: This detects the problem after the fact.

questions.explanation: Enforce required step ordering with prerequisite gates based on tool-recorded state.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to explore a risky refactor approach in a session without losing the clean state of the current analysis session, which they may want to continue down a different path. What should they do?

options.text: Fork the session, and try the risky approach in the fork, leaving the original session intact.
options.why: Forking branches the conversation from a shared baseline.

options.text: Continue in the same session and undo it if needed.
options.why: The context gets contaminated by the abandoned path.

options.text: Copy the transcript into a text file.
options.why: This is manual and loses session state.

options.text: Use plan mode.
options.why: Plan mode doesn't create an independent branch.

questions.explanation: Session forking is the mechanism for exploring alternatives from the same starting point.

questions.stem: The deployment-catalog MCP server exposes a tool called `query` with the description "Query the catalog." The agent rarely uses it, and when it does, it passes malformed filters. Which TWO changes improve this most? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Rename it to something specific, such as `find_service_deployments`.
options.why: Specific names clarify purpose and reduce confusion with other tools.

options.text: Expand the description with the filter syntax, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it versus the wiki tool.
options.why: Detailed descriptions drive correct selection and inputs.

options.text: Force it with `tool_choice` on every turn.
options.why: This breaks other tasks.

options.text: Hide it behind a Bash wrapper script.
options.why: This makes it less structured and harder to select correctly.

options.text: Remove the parameter schema so any input is accepted.
options.why: Inputs get worse, not better.

questions.explanation: Generic tool names and thin descriptions cause both selection and input errors. Rename tools and describe them thoroughly.

questions.stem: A "read-only Q&A" mode of the assistant should answer questions but never modify the codebase. How should its tools be configured?

options.text: Allow only the read-oriented tools (Read, Grep, Glob, read-only MCP tools) through `allowedTools`, and exclude Write, Edit and unrestricted Bash.
options.why: Tool scoping enforces least privilege deterministically.

options.text: Keep all tools but instruct the model not to modify anything.
options.why: This is probabilistic.

options.text: Keep Write but log every write.
options.why: This detects the damage after the fact.

options.text: Use a smaller model, which writes less often.
options.why: This is nonsensical as a control.

questions.explanation: Restrict tools to what the role needs, which enforces boundaries structurally.

questions.stem: The CI reviewer analyses large PRs in one pass and misses issues in files late in the diff. Which decomposition is most appropriate?

options.text: Run per-file analysis passes, then a cross-file integration pass that checks how the changes interact (interfaces, shared state).
options.why: Local passes plus an integration pass prevent attention dilution.

options.text: Review only the first 10 files.
options.why: This leaves coverage gaps.

options.text: Concatenate the files in random order.
options.why: This doesn't fix dilution.

options.text: Use a single pass with a reminder to "check every file".
options.why: This is vague guidance.

questions.explanation: Split large analyses into per-file passes plus an integration pass.

questions.stem: The CI bot can auto-approve PRs. Policy says that PRs touching `payments/` must always get human review. What is the most reliable enforcement?

options.text: Deterministic pipeline logic (for example CODEOWNERS or a CI check) that blocks auto-approval when the diff touches `payments/`, regardless of the model's output.
options.why: Hard policy belongs in code, not in model judgement.

options.text: A prompt line: "never approve payments changes".
options.why: This is probabilistic.

options.text: Ask the model to self-report whether payments files were touched.
options.why: That is self-reported.

options.text: A monthly audit of approvals.
options.why: This catches violations after the fact.

questions.explanation: Enforce mandatory human-in-the-loop rules programmatically around the model.

questions.stem: Which statement about running Claude Code in GitHub Actions is correct?

options.text: Run it non-interactively with `-p`. Committed CLAUDE.md and `.claude/` configuration in the checkout provide project context, and structured output can be requested with `--output-format json` (optionally with `--json-schema`).
options.why: These are the documented CI building blocks.

options.text: CI must use a special "Claude CI" binary that ignores CLAUDE.md.
options.why: No such binary exists.

options.text: Interactive mode is fine in CI as long as the job's timeout is long enough.
options.why: It waits for input forever.

options.text: Claude Code can only output plain text in CI.
options.why: JSON output is supported.

questions.explanation: The CI integration rests on `-p`, project memory, and structured output flags.

questions.stem: Security wants the CI reviewer and the CI test-writer to behave differently: the reviewer must never modify files. What is the cleanest setup?

options.text: Run separate invocations, each with its own prompt and its own allowed-tools configuration (the reviewer limited to read-only tools, the test-writer allowed to write in test directories).
options.why: Separate, scoped instances apply least privilege and independent review.

options.text: Run one invocation that does both, with a prompt saying "don't modify files while reviewing".
options.why: This is probabilistic, and the roles are mixed.

options.text: Give both full permissions and revert unwanted changes afterwards.
options.why: This is unsafe.

options.text: Run only the test-writer and skip reviews.
options.why: It loses a required capability.

questions.explanation: Give each CI role its own instance and tool permissions, which separates concerns and enforces boundaries.

questions.stem: Findings are posted through a `report_findings` tool with a schema. Some findings have `severity: "urgent"`, which isn't one of the expected values, and this breaks the dashboard. What is the best schema-level fix?

options.text: Define `severity` as an enum (for example `critical`, `major`, `minor`) in the tool's JSON schema, so only valid values can be produced.
options.why: Enums constrain the values at the schema level.

options.text: Map unknown values in the dashboard.
options.why: This is downstream patching and stays brittle.

options.text: Ask the model to use standard severities.
options.why: This is probabilistic.

options.text: Remove severity from the schema.
options.why: This loses needed information.

questions.explanation: Use enums in schemas for constrained categorical fields, with an `other` or `unclear` value where appropriate.

questions.stem: To reduce missed bugs, a developer proposes letting the reviewer use extended thinking in the same session that generated the code fix, instead of running a separate review. What is the main weakness of this proposal?

options.text: More thinking in the same context still carries the original generation's reasoning and assumptions. An independent instance without that context is more likely to catch the errors.
options.why: Independence matters more than extra deliberation for self-review.

options.text: Extended thinking isn't available in CI.
options.why: That isn't the core issue.

options.text: Extended thinking makes outputs non-JSON.
options.why: Unrelated.

options.text: There is no weakness. It is equivalent to an independent review.
options.why: Shared context creates shared blind spots.

questions.explanation: Independent review instances beat both self-review and same-session extended thinking.

questions.stem: The extraction flow is: classify document type → extract fields with the type-specific schema → validate → post or route. Which architecture best fits this?

options.text: A prompt chain with deterministic code between the steps: classification output selects the schema, and code validates and routes.
options.why: Known, sequential stages suit chaining with programmatic glue.

options.text: One prompt that classifies, extracts, validates and decides posting at once.
options.why: This is hard to validate and debug, and lets the model decide the posting.

options.text: A dynamic multi-agent coordinator for every document.
options.why: This is overkill for a fixed pipeline.

options.text: Let the model choose its own schema per document.
options.why: This is inconsistent for downstream systems.

questions.explanation: Fixed pipelines use prompt chaining, and deterministic code handles schema selection, validation and routing.

questions.stem: Finance requires that no invoice over €50,000 is auto-posted to the ERP, whatever the extraction confidence. Where should this rule live?

options.text: In the deterministic posting code, which checks the extracted, validated amount and routes high-value invoices to human approval.
options.why: Financial controls must be enforced in code.

options.text: In the extraction prompt: "flag invoices over €50,000".
options.why: This is probabilistic.

options.text: In the model's confidence threshold.
options.why: Confidence isn't the rule. Amount is.

options.text: In a weekly finance report of large postings.
options.why: This catches the problem after posting.

questions.explanation: Hard business rules sit in deterministic code around the model.

questions.stem: The model sometimes extracts a customs form's "declared value" from the "insured value" box. Which schema addition makes such mistakes easier to detect and debug?

options.text: A field recording where each key value was found (for example `declared_value_source: "box 22"`, or a `detected_pattern`), so validators and reviewers can check the provenance.
options.why: Provenance and self-check fields make extraction errors visible.

options.text: A free-text `notes` field with no structure.
options.why: It can't be checked reliably.

options.text: Removing the insured value from the schema.
options.why: That doesn't stop confusion with the box on the page.

options.text: A higher temperature for more varied extractions.
options.why: Counterproductive.

questions.explanation: Fields such as the source location or `detected_pattern` support validation and debugging of extractions.

questions.stem: Dates appear as `03/04/2026`, `4 Mar 2026` and `2026-03-04` across suppliers from different countries. Downstream systems need ISO 8601. Which TWO measures are most appropriate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: State an explicit format-normalisation rule in the prompt or schema description (output ISO 8601; interpret ambiguous day/month using the document's country or locale), with examples.
options.why: Explicit normalisation rules with examples guide consistent output.

options.text: Validate in code that dates parse as ISO 8601, and flag ambiguous ones (for example a missing locale) for review.
options.why: Code-level validation catches residual errors.

options.text: Let downstream systems guess the format.
options.why: Ambiguous dates get misparsed.

options.text: Store dates as free text.
options.why: This breaks downstream integration.

options.text: Always assume US format.
options.why: Wrong for most non-US suppliers.

questions.explanation: Combine prompt or schema normalisation rules with deterministic validation.

questions.stem: Human reviewers can handle 1,500 documents a week, but the pipeline flags 6,000 as needing review. What is the best way to make review sustainable without losing safety?

options.text: Use calibrated, field-level confidence and validation results to route only the genuinely risky records (low-confidence critical fields, failed reconciliations, conflicts), and monitor auto-posted records with stratified sampling.
options.why: Targeted routing plus sampling balances workload and safety.

options.text: Randomly select 1,500 of the 6,000 for review and auto-post the rest.
options.why: This auto-posts high-risk records at random.

options.text: Lower the confidence threshold until only 1,500 are flagged, without validating the change.
options.why: Uncalibrated threshold changes hide risk.

options.text: Stop processing until more reviewers are hired.
options.why: This ignores the better routing that is available.

questions.explanation: Human review should be targeted with calibrated confidence and validations, and backed by stratified sampling.

questions.stem: The extraction step calls Claude with three tools available: `extract_invoice`, `extract_bol` and `extract_customs`. The document type has already been determined by the classification step. How should `tool_choice` be set?

options.text: Force the specific tool for the known type, for example `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}`.
options.why: When the correct tool is known deterministically, force it.

options.text: `auto`, to let the model decide.
options.why: The model could answer in text or pick the wrong schema.

options.text: `any`, so some extraction tool is used.
options.why: The model might pick the wrong schema.

options.text: `none`, and parse JSON from the text.
options.why: This loses schema enforcement.

questions.explanation: Use the forced tool choice when the code already knows which structured output it needs.
